title: Grandpa Mensah’s Secret to a Peaceful Retirement

pages.text: On the first Tuesday of the month, twelve-year-old Efua and her brother Kojo sat on the veranda helping Grandpa Mensah prune young mango saplings in pots. Grandpa Mensah’s mobile phone chimed softly. He smiled at the screen and said to Grandma Mansa, ‘Our monthly pension has arrived, let us pay the electricity bill and buy Efua and Kojo’s new maths sets.’
sentences: On the first Tuesday of the month, twelve-year-old Efua and her brother Kojo sat on the veranda helping Grandpa Mensah prune young mango saplings in pots.
Grandpa Mensah’s mobile phone chimed softly.
He smiled at the screen and said to Grandma Mansa, ‘Our monthly pension has arrived, let us pay the electricity bill and buy Efua and Kojo’s new maths sets.’
pages.alt: On a sunny garden veranda, retired Grandpa Mensah smiles at a notification on his phone while Grandma Mansa, Efua and Kojo tend potted mango saplings.

pages.text: Kojo looked puzzled. ‘Grandpa, you retired from teaching five years ago, and Grandma Mansa handed over her market stall last year. Who is still paying you every month when you no longer go to work?’ Grandpa Mensah chuckled and tapped a tall, fruiting mango tree in the middle of the yard. ‘Thirty-five years ago, Kojo, our younger selves planted the seeds that are feeding us today!’
sentences: Kojo looked puzzled.
‘Grandpa, you retired from teaching five years ago, and Grandma Mansa handed over her market stall last year.
Who is still paying you every month when you no longer go to work?’ Grandpa Mensah chuckled and tapped a tall, fruiting mango tree in the middle of the yard.
‘Thirty-five years ago, Kojo, our younger selves planted the seeds that are feeding us today!’
pages.alt: Grandpa Mensah points to a tall, fruit-laden mango tree in the courtyard while Kojo and Efua listen in curiosity.

pages.text: ‘A pension,’ explained Grandpa Mensah, ‘is a long-term retirement fund built during your working years so you have steady income when you are older and can no longer work full-time. Every month when I taught in the classroom, a small fraction of my salary, together with a statutory contribution from my employer, went straight into my pension fund before I could spend it.’
sentences: ‘A pension,’ explained Grandpa Mensah, ‘is a long-term retirement fund built during your working years so you have steady income when you are older and can no longer work full-time.
Every month when I taught in the classroom, a small fraction of my salary, together with a statutory contribution from my employer, went straight into my pension fund before I could spend it.’
pages.alt: Grandpa Mensah shows his old teacher’s payslip binder alongside a diagram of monthly contributions flowing into a retirement pot.

pages.text: ‘Did your pension money just sit still in a box for thirty-five years?’ asked Efua. ‘Not at all!’ said Grandpa Mensah. ‘The pension fund invested our contributions carefully so they grew through compounding, earning returns not only on our original savings, but also on the previous years’ returns! Let us do a quick calculation in your notebook, Kojo.’

‘Not at all!’ said Grandpa Mensah.
‘The pension fund invested our contributions carefully so they grew through compounding, earning returns not only on our original savings, but also on the previous years’ returns!
Let us do a quick calculation in your notebook, Kojo.’
pages.alt: Efua and Kojo open their notebooks as Grandpa Mensah prepares to demonstrate compound growth.

pages.text: ‘Suppose you place one thousand cedis into a fund that earns ten percent a year,’ said Grandpa Mensah. ‘In Year 1, ten percent of one thousand cedis is one hundred cedis, so your balance grows to one thousand one hundred cedis. In Year 2, you earn ten percent on the full one thousand one hundred cedis, which is one hundred and ten cedis! One thousand one hundred plus one hundred and ten equals one thousand two hundred and ten cedis.’
sentences: ‘Suppose you place one thousand cedis into a fund that earns ten percent a year,’ said Grandpa Mensah.
‘In Year 1, ten percent of one thousand cedis is one hundred cedis, so your balance grows to one thousand one hundred cedis.
In Year 2, you earn ten percent on the full one thousand one hundred cedis, which is one hundred and ten cedis!
One thousand one hundred plus one hundred and ten equals one thousand two hundred and ten cedis.’
pages.alt: Kojo writes the Year 1 (1,100 cedis) and Year 2 (1,210 cedis) compounding numbers while Grandpa Mensah points to the extra 10 cedis earned on Year 1’s return.

pages.text: ‘That extra ten cedis in Year 2 looks small at first,’ said Efua, ‘but what happens over thirty or forty years of working and adding new contributions every single month?’ ‘It snowballs!’ said Grandpa Mensah. ‘When you start early in your twenties instead of waiting until your fifties, compounding has decades to work for you.’
sentences: ‘That extra ten cedis in Year 2 looks small at first,’ said Efua, ‘but what happens over thirty or forty years of working and adding new contributions every single month?’ ‘It snowballs!’ said Grandpa Mensah.
‘When you start early in your twenties instead of waiting until your fifties, compounding has decades to work for you.’
pages.alt: A visual chart compares a steep rising curve from starting early at age 22 with a much smaller curve from starting late at age 50.

pages.text: Then Kojo turned to Grandma Mansa. ‘Grandma, Grandpa was a government school headmaster, so his employer sent his contributions automatically. What about you? You worked for yourself in the market!’ Grandma Mansa smiled proudly. ‘That is the beauty of Ghana’s Three-Tier Pension System, regulated by the National Pensions Regulatory Authority, the NPRA!’
sentences: Then Kojo turned to Grandma Mansa.
‘Grandma, Grandpa was a government school headmaster, so his employer sent his contributions automatically.
What about you?
You worked for yourself in the market!’ Grandma Mansa smiled proudly.
‘That is the beauty of Ghana’s Three-Tier Pension System, regulated by the National Pensions Regulatory Authority, the NPRA!’
pages.alt: Grandma Mansa holds up three stacked woven baskets representing Ghana’s Three-Tier Pension System.

pages.text: Grandma Mansa tapped the bottom basket first. ‘Tier 1 is the mandatory basic national social security scheme managed by SSNIT, the Social Security and National Insurance Trust. It pays retired workers like Grandpa a steady monthly pension for life. The middle basket, Tier 2, is a mandatory occupational scheme managed by licensed private trustees that pays a lump sum when you retire.’
sentences: Grandma Mansa tapped the bottom basket first.
‘Tier 1 is the mandatory basic national social security scheme managed by SSNIT, the Social Security and National Insurance Trust.
It pays retired workers like Grandpa a steady monthly pension for life.
The middle basket, Tier 2, is a mandatory occupational scheme managed by licensed private trustees that pays a lump sum when you retire.’
pages.alt: Grandma Mansa points to the first two baskets representing Tier 1 (SSNIT monthly pension) and Tier 2 (lump-sum occupational benefit).

pages.text: Then Grandma Mansa lifted the top basket. ‘And Tier 3 includes voluntary provident funds and personal pension schemes! Because I was a self-employed market trader in the informal sector, I joined an NPRA-licensed Tier 3 personal pension scheme and contributed faithfully every week from my market profits. Now I receive my own retirement income too, without anyone having to beg or borrow!’
sentences: Then Grandma Mansa lifted the top basket.
‘And Tier 3 includes voluntary provident funds and personal pension schemes!
Because I was a self-employed market trader in the informal sector, I joined an NPRA-licensed Tier 3 personal pension scheme and contributed faithfully every week from my market profits.
Now I receive my own retirement income too, without anyone having to beg or borrow!’
pages.alt: Grandma Mansa lifts the third basket proudly, showing how informal-sector traders and self-employed workers save through Tier 3 pensions.

pages.text: ‘Does inflation affect pensions too?’ asked Efua, remembering how prices rise over decades. ‘Very good question, Efua!’ said Grandpa Mensah. ‘Because prices rise over twenty or thirty years, pension funds invest in assets that aim to grow faster than inflation, and wise workers also make extra voluntary Tier 3 contributions so their retirement income keeps its purchasing power.’
sentences: ‘Does inflation affect pensions too?’ asked Efua, remembering how prices rise over decades.
‘Very good question, Efua!’ said Grandpa Mensah.

‘Because prices rise over twenty or thirty years, pension funds invest in assets that aim to grow faster than inflation, and wise workers also make extra voluntary Tier 3 contributions so their retirement income keeps its purchasing power.’
pages.alt: Efua asks about inflation while Grandpa Mensah shows how Tier 3 voluntary top-ups strengthen retirement security.

pages.text: Grandpa Mensah handed Efua and Kojo each a small potted mango sapling to plant near the school fence. ‘Supporting elderly relatives is a cherished Ghanaian value,’ he told them gently, ‘and preparing your own pension early is one of the greatest gifts you can give your future self and your children. Plant early, contribute steadily, and let time help your tree grow!’

pages.alt: Efua and Kojo each hold a young mango sapling beside Grandpa Mensah and Grandma Mansa under the shade of the tall mango tree.

activities.question: If 1,000 cedis earns 10% per year, why does it grow to 1,210 cedis after 2 years instead of 1,200 cedis?
options: In Year 2 you earn 10% on 1,100 cedis (110 cedis), compounding the growth
The bank made a counting mistake of 10 cedis
Ten percent of 1,000 cedis is 105 cedis each year

activities.definition: Earning returns on both your original savings and past returns
distractors: Spending all your savings at the end of every month
Keeping coins inside an unsealed clay pot

activities.question: How did Grandma Mansa, a self-employed market trader, build a formal pension in Ghana?
options: By contributing regularly to an NPRA-regulated Tier 3 personal pension
By waiting for a surprise lottery prize at age sixty
Only government teachers are allowed to save for retirement
activities.explanation: Ghana’s Tier 3 personal pension schemes allow self-employed and informal-sector workers to build regulated retirement savings.

activities.question: In Ghana’s Three-Tier Pension System, what do Tier 1 (SSNIT) and Tier 2 provide at retirement?
options: Tier 1 pays a monthly pension; Tier 2 pays a lump sum
Both tiers only pay in mango saplings
Tier 1 is only for children; Tier 2 is only for tourists
activities.explanation: Tier 1 (SSNIT) provides a monthly pension for life, while Tier 2 provides a lump-sum occupational payout.

activities.prompt: Order the stages of building a peaceful retirement.
items: Start contributing a slice of income early in your working life.
Let contributions grow over decades through compounding in Tiers 1–3.
Receive steady monthly pension and lump-sum benefits in retirement.

activities.prompt: Why did Grandpa Mensah compare saving for retirement to planting a mango sapling decades before you need the shade and fruit?

glossary.definition: A long-term fund built during a person’s working years to provide regular income during retirement
Having stepped back from full-time employment in older age after years of work
The process by which investment returns themselves earn additional returns over time
Required by law for eligible workers and employers
Chosen freely, such as extra personal pension contributions in Tier 3
